name: Fatima Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice with a contractor that the power company hires to upgrade lines, mostly on the edge of the city where they're building new housing estates. So a lot of my days are setting new poles, hanging transformers, and running bigger wires so every house can have an electric car charger. I'm usually on the ground, rigging and sending gear up, and I do some climbing with a journeyman watching me like a hawk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the problem-solving, figuring out the order of a job so nobody's standing around. What wears me out is the physical side, honestly, I'm not as strong as the guys and my arms are dead by Thursday. I've been doing extra gym sessions with Sam, my partner, she's a physiotherapist so she's very strict about my shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit surprised, but okay, it's still a useful tool. I use it every day for planning and studying, so I'd say people shouldn't throw it away just because it didn't change the world. I'd probably say that in a group chat, I'm not big on posting publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I get to keep my plans as they are. Finish the apprenticeship, keep doing my weekend drone photography for estate agents, maybe grow that a bit. My little drone business would honestly get more out of a plateau than my day job would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on both tracks. Keep my savings at around four months, put the drone money into a separate account, and maybe buy a better camera for the drone this year. I'd keep using AI to edit photos and write quotes for clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost a bit bored, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drone business. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: During my first year I got my drone licence for fun, and a neighbour who sells houses asked me to shoot one from above. Now I do two or three a month at weekends. It's not huge, maybe a few hundred a month, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the company might not invest in new kit for us if the AI hype dies. They were talking about drones for inspecting lines, and I wanted in on that. In this picture that might go on the back burner.

S0.say: I'd say I'm surprised, but it's still a useful tool and people shouldn't throw it away. I'd say that in a group chat rather than posting publicly.
S0.think: It means I keep my plans as they are: finish the apprenticeship and grow my weekend drone photography. That little business would get more out of a plateau than my day job would.
S0.do: Keeps going on both tracks, holding savings at about four months and keeping drone earnings in a separate account. Buys a better drone camera and uses AI to edit photos and write quotes.
S0.quote: My little drone business would honestly get more out of a plateau than my day job would.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima already runs a small side business and uses AI daily for it, so she sees the plateau through two lenses. She's frank about finding the physical side of the job hard and is working on it. Her only disappointment is that company drone inspections might stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and the smart move is to get ahead of it. At work I'd tell the other apprentices to start learning the new kit now instead of waiting. I wouldn't say much about politics, I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Lines aren't going anywhere, and the company will need people who can run drones, read the AI fault reports and still climb a pole. I'm not the strongest on the crew, but I might be the one who knows what the computer's trying to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my supervisor in the first month and ask to be on the drone inspection trial. I'd do every online course I can find on grid sensors and inspection software in the evenings. I'd keep the photography going as a side income and keep my savings steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the job's growing in my direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices who don't want to learn the new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try not to be preachy about it. I'd probably show them on my phone how I use it, like how it reads a pole inspection photo and flags rot. Some of them would roll their eyes, and that's fine, I'm not their mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's patients, actually, more than my crew. A lot of them are older and already confused by the apps the clinic makes them use. Sam spends half her time helping them log in.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big shift and the smart move is to get ahead of it. I'd tell other apprentices to start learning the new kit now instead of waiting.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because the company will need people who can run drones, read AI fault reports and still climb. I'm not the strongest, but I might understand what the computer's saying.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor in the first month to join the drone inspection trial. Takes online courses on grid sensors and inspection software in the evenings and keeps her photography side income going.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, as if the job were growing her way.
S1.quote: I'm not the strongest on the crew, but I might be the one who knows what the computer's trying to say.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima sees steady disruption as a chance to make up for her physical weakness with tech skills. She'd move first and fast, asking to join the trial within a month. She's careful not to lecture colleagues, and her worry turns to her partner's older patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be practical about what we do next. I'd tell people not to waste the two years arguing about whether it's fair. In private I'd say it's terrifying, but I wouldn't say that at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think being good with tech buys me maybe a year or two, not a career. If AI can do almost any job, it can fly the drone and edit the photos too, so the side business goes as well. I've spent two years building two careers, and in this picture both of them hit the wall at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd apply to the robot makers and the companies that'll install robots on the grid, because someone has to set them up and fix them in the first years. I'd push my savings from four months to six by cutting back and putting all the drone money in, and I'd use AI every night to learn whatever those companies need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but definitely running on adrenaline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd apply to the robot companies. Is that a bit like helping replace your own crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've thought about that, and I don't love it. But if the robots are coming in two years either way, I'd rather be the one setting them up safely than standing next to them with nothing to do. I'd feel guilty for about a week and then I'd pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say slow down and think it through, that's how we work, she's the steady one. Then she'd help me redo my CV at the kitchen table at midnight.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening, so let's be practical and not waste two years arguing about whether it's fair. Privately it's terrifying, but I wouldn't say that at work.
S2.think: Being good with tech buys me maybe a year or two, not a career. If AI can fly drones and edit photos, my side business hits the wall at the same time as my day job.
S2.do: Applies straight away to robot makers and grid robot installers, using AI each night to learn their skills. Raises savings from four to six months by cutting back and putting all drone income aside.
S2.feel: Anxious and running on adrenaline, but not frozen.
S2.quote: I've spent two years building two careers, and in this picture both of them hit the wall at the same time.
S2.fieldNote: Fatima's two-track plan collapses at once in this picture, which shakes her. She'd still be the first to act, even applying to the companies that would replace her crew, and she admits the guilt plainly. Her partner is the steadying influence who helps rather than stops her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready if you start now. At work I'd tell people to pick up one new skill a year. Online I'd maybe share a few courses that are actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years feels okay for me. I'd finish my apprenticeship, get proper experience with drones and sensors, and be in a good spot to move into robot setup and repair before the big wave. The side business probably fades, but I'd have time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the apprenticeship and get on the drone inspection team. Year two or three, I'd look at moving to whatever city the grid robot companies set up in, even if it's a few hours away. I'd keep saving and keep learning every evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But more like before an exam than before a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move cities. What would that mean for you and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a big conversation. Sam's built up her client list here over five years. I'd ask her to give up her patients for my robots, and I'm not sure that's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the drone money in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running it until the robots can do it better, then sell the kit. Good drones hold their value for a while. I'd put that money into savings or a course.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now, picking up one new skill a year. I might share a few good courses online.
S3.think: Five years feels okay: I'd qualify, get experience with drones and sensors, and move into robot setup and repair before the big wave. The side business probably fades, but I'd see it coming.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and joins the drone inspection team in year one. Considers moving to a city where grid robot companies set up in year two or three, while saving and learning every evening.
S3.feel: Uneasy, more like before an exam than before a crash.
S3.quote: I'd ask her to give up her patients for my robots, and I'm not sure that's fair.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her a workable ladder, but the cost lands on her relationship: a move would mean her partner giving up her clients. She names that tension herself without being prompted. She'd wind down the drone business in an orderly way rather than cling to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to plan properly, so there's no excuse not to. At work I'd say this is the time to get two or three skills, not just one. I'd also tell my friends to think about owning a bit of what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel pretty good. I'd have years to build up drone and robot experience, and I could start putting money into the companies making the robots. If the robots end up doing my job, I'd at least like to own a small slice of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, join the inspection team, and save up for a two-year technical diploma in automation by year four. I'd start putting maybe a hundred a month into a fund of robotics and energy companies. I'd keep the drone business as long as it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A hundred a month into shares. Have you done anything like that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a small savings account so far. I'd read up first, and probably use an AI tool to explain the basics, then start small. I'm not trying to get rich, I just don't want to be on the wrong side of the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything else, like where you live or family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I have talked about kids in a few years. Ten years warning wouldn't stop that, but it'd make me want both of us to have solid savings first. We'd probably wait an extra year or two.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty to plan properly, so there's no excuse not to. I'd tell people to get two or three skills and think about owning a bit of what's coming.
S4.think: I'd feel pretty good: I'd have years to build drone and robot experience and could invest in the companies making the robots. If they do my job, I'd like to own a small slice of them.
S4.do: Finishes her apprenticeship, joins the inspection team and saves for a two-year automation diploma by year four. Starts putting about a hundred a month into a fund of robotics and energy companies.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, as it feels like something she can plan for.
S4.quote: I'm not trying to get rich, I just don't want to be on the wrong side of the machine.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Fatima's pragmatism turns towards ownership: she'd invest a little in the robots rather than campaign against them. Her plans are concrete and staged by year. She and her partner would delay children a year or two to build savings first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both my job and my side business go at once and there's no time to build a third thing. What would help is fast, short courses for the new jobs, paid for by the companies bringing in the robots, and some kind of income support for the gap months.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in the trade. I fought hard to get into this, and now the robots might make strength not matter, which in a weird way helps me. It's strange to be worried and a little bit pleased at the same time.

headlineQuote: If the robots end up doing my job, I'd at least like to own a small slice of the robots.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old apprentice with a contractor upgrading lines on new housing estates, still building the strength the job demands and running a small weekend drone photography business on the side. She uses AI every day and moves first whenever new tools appear. She is calm about the plateau and steady disruption, seeing her tech skills as making up for her physical ones. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because her job and side business would collapse together, though she'd still act fast by applying to robot companies. With five or ten years she plans a staged move into automation, would consider a city move that strains her relationship, and would buy a small stake in the robots themselves.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her job and her side business would go at once with no time to build something new.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, short courses for the new jobs paid for by the companies bringing in robots, and income support for the gap months.
